title: Surge valve and admission controller PRD (sketch)
content:
Purpose
This is a working PRD sketch for a new Dedicated Capacity control plane component we are calling the 'Surge Valve' + Admission Controller. Goal: give tenants predictable protection during short, sharp demand spikes while preserving high utilization and strong isolation guarantees.

Why a new pattern?
- Existing approaches (large static reserves, pure token-credit bursts) either waste capacity or expose noisy-neighbor failure modes.
- We need a lightweight admission layer that can dynamically shape short-term pressure (seconds->minutes) and gracefully degrade tenant fidelity without global outages.

Problem statement (real-world signals)
- Several customers experience micro-spikes (hundreds of concurrent short requests) that blow tail latency even when long-run utilization looks fine.
- Autoscalers that react on minutes-level metrics are too slow for microbursts.
- Hard isolation (node pinning) is too expensive for many tenants; soft isolation leaks into other tenants because caches and KV hot paths aren’t partitioned.

High-level goals
- Protect latency SLOs for latency-critical tenants during surges.
- Allow opportunistic, short-lived capacity sharing to increase overall utilization.
- Provide clear isolation knobs (soft->hard) for customers with different risk profiles.
- Expose simple UX with conservative defaults and safe rollback.

Non-goals
- Replace existing autoscaler for sustained traffic growth. This is complementary (short-window smoothing + admission).
- Solve every noisy-neighbor mode (we will iterate with SRE for hardware-level isolation).

Conceptual model
- Reservoirs: small ephemeral "micro-reservoirs" per tenant that accumulate allotment for bursty work over short windows (e.g., 60s). The reservoir is a leaky bucket with configurable capacity and refill rules.
- Surge Valve: an admission policy that closes or modulates admissions based on a combination of internal signals — reservoir fill, node pressure, KV cache hit pressure, and tail latency gauges. Valve state: open / throttled / restricted.
- Admission Controller: two-stage filter at the edge of Dedicated pools: (1) fast-path admissions (low-latency, token-checked) (2) queued/batched admissions (for non-critical or large-batch jobs).
- Fuse layers (isolation primitives):
  - Soft Fuse: token-bucket throttles + ephemeral reservoir limits. Cheap, multitenant friendly.
  - Cache Affinity Fuse: enforce per-tenant KV cache weighting to avoid colding other tenants.
  - Hard Fuse: node/slot pinning and explicit capacity carveouts — used only for highest-tier customers.

Autoscaling interplay
- Autoscaler remains primary for medium/long horizons. The Surge Valve sits in front of the runtime and can temporarily throttle or re-route to alternative model variants (quantized or smaller model) rather than scale out.
- Autoscaler signals to Surge Valve: predicted warm-up windows, available warm-pool count. Surge Valve uses these to adjust aggressiveness (e.g., delay throttling if warm pool will be available within X seconds).

Admission policy (default heuristic)
1) If reservoir_fill >= 25% and node_pressure < 70% -> accept on fast-path.
2) If tail_latency_99 > configured_slo_threshold and reservoir_fill < 15% -> move to throttled mode: accept only high-priority tokens, queue others or route to degraded variant.
3) If node_pressure > 90% -> restricted mode: only top-tier tenants and background batch jobs allowed; opportunistic lanes closed.
Notes: thresholds are configurable per-tenant and per-pool. We will expose two presets: conservative (lower chance of degraded experience) and efficient (higher utilization tolerance).

Burst options (user-configurable patterns)
- Microburst windowing: burst allowance defined as a curve (time vs units) rather than a single credit. This curve decays with a configurable half-life — prevents one-off spike from granting permanent high allowance.
- Graceful downgrade routes: admission controller can route accepted requests to lower-fidelity variants (lower token cost), to cached completion responses (when prefix matches), or to queued execution with an SLA on completion time. Tenants can opt into auto-degrade; Default: attempt same fidelity first, degrade only if admission would otherwise be rejected.
- Cross-tenant lending (opt-in): low-risk tenants can supply small, revocable credits into a shared micro-reservoir for a pool of opportunistic capacity. Lenders can be repaid or penalized in long-term priority. This is opt-in and clearly visible in billing.

Isolation controls (config + ops)
- Config knobs per tenant: reservoir_size, refill_rate, valve_sensitivity, downgrade_policy, cache_affinity_weight, hard_fuse (boolean).
- Default per-customer template based on SLA tier (standard, premium, regulated).
- Hard isolation workflow: request via support -> model and dataset approvals -> node affinity labels applied -> KV cache partitioning enabled -> monitoring escalations.

Observability and signals (telemetry)
- New metrics to emit: valve_state, reservoir_fill_pct, admission_accept_rate, admission_queue_depth, degraded_route_rate, cache_pressure_index, fairness_index (per-pool), tail_latency_p95/p99 per-tenant, valve_reject_reasons (categorical).
- Charts: per-tenant valve pressure timeline, cross-tenant fairness heatmap, correlation dashboards between cache_pressure and tail_latency.
- Alerts: auto-escalate when valve enters restricted mode for > 2 minutes for > 5% of tenants in a pool.

UX & Console exposure
- Simple slider for Surge Valve sensitivity with three presets: Safe / Balanced / Aggressive. Advanced page for per-knob override.
- Rollout controls: canary, gradual percentage, auto-rollback threshold (customer-visible SLO regression > X%).
- Clear UI explanation and recommended defaults for regulated customers (suggest enabling hard_fuse).

Operational playbook (runbook sketch)
- Detect: Valve enters restricted state -> check upstream autoscaler signals and warm-pool counts.
- Remediate: if warm-pool shortage, trigger pre-warm job or manual warm up; if KV cache thrashing, isolate offending tenant/process.
- Short-term: enable temporary cap increases for affected premium tenants or route to degraded variants.
- Postmortem: capture reservoir drain patterns and adjust refill curves.

Rollout plan
1) Build minimal admission controller + valve_state metric behind feature flag (internal-only).
2) Internal dogfood with infra and a few product teams (2–4 tenants). Collect telemetry for 4 weeks.
3) Opt-in beta for <10 customers with varied profiles.
4) Gradual GA with console defaults and support playbook.

Open questions / risks
- How fine-grained should default reservoirs be? Per-team, per-route, per-token-type? (initial plan: per-tenant, with route-level overrides).
- Billing visibility for cross-tenant lending and degraded routes (need clear pricing language).
- Risk of complexity: too many knobs -> misconfiguration; mitigate with sensible presets and guardrails.
- Multi-region semantics: valve decisions must respect region boundaries to avoid cross-region routing complexity.

Next steps (concrete)
- Engineering spike for admission controller prototype (2 sprints) to validate low-latency checks and state propagation. Owner: Daniel Ortiz.
- Telemetry schema draft and dashboard template. Owner: Maya Liu.
- Legal + finance review for billing semantics of lending and degraded route charges. Owner: Tomás Rivera.

Notes to self / discussion fragments
- Consider half-life tuned by tenant traffic periodicity.
- Think about a compact API label: valveMode or admissionProfile.
- Who owns the fallthrough degraded variant catalog? Product + Applied ML to propose conservative variants per-model.

References
- similar pattern inspiration: TCP congestion window + leaky-bucket rate shaping; CDN request admission heuristics; database admission controllers for transactional bursts.

--end of sketch--
